k​tkt-Safety: Graph Release via kk-Anonymity and tt-Closeness (Technical Report)

Weilong Ren    Kambiz Ghazinour       Xiang Lian Thanks:  W. Ren is with Shenzhen Institute of Computing Sciences, Shenzhen, China. E-mail: renweilong@sics.ac.cn K. Ghazinour is with the State University of New York, Canton, NY, USA. E-mail: ghazinourk@canton.edu X. Lian is with the Department of Computer Science, Kent State University, Kent, Ohio, USA. E-mail: xlian@kent.edu
Abstract

In a wide spectrum of real-world applications, it is very important to analyze and mine graph data such as social networks, communication networks, citation networks, and so on. However, the release of such graph data often raises privacy issue, and the graph privacy preservation has recently drawn much attention from the database community. While prior works on graph privacy preservation mainly focused on protecting the privacy of either the graph structure only or vertex attributes only, in this paper, we propose a novel mechanism for graph privacy preservation by considering attacks from both graph structures and vertex attributes, which transforms the original graph to a so-called k​tkt-safe graph, via kk-anonymity and tt-closeness. We prove that the generation of a k​tkt-safe graph is NP-hard, therefore, we propose a feasible framework for effectively and efficiently anonymizing a graph with low anonymization cost. In particular, we design a cost-model-based graph partitioning approach to enable our proposed divide-and-conquer strategy for the graph anonymization, and propose effective optimization techniques such as pruning method and a tree synopsis to improve the anonymization efficiency over large-scale graphs. Extensive experiments have been conducted to verify the efficiency and effectiveness of our proposed k​tkt-safe graph generation approach on both real and synthetic data sets.

Index Terms: 
k​tkt-Safety, kk-Anonymity, tt-Closeness.

I Introduction

The rapid development of social-network applications such as Twitter, Facebook, MySpace, and Friendster has brought a great opportunity for researchers and industries to better explore and understand social behaviors hidden in the world of human beings. To do so, some organizations or companies (e.g., Facebook) may need to release social-network data to the public, where the released data may contain users’ privacy information (e.g., salary and relationships with other users). To protect such privacy information from leakage, some critical identifiers (e.g., name and social security numbers) that can uniquely identify users are usually removed before publishing. However, simply removing these identifiers cannot prevent attackers from locating a user (node) in social networks, since a user can also be identified by one’s quasi-identifier (e.g., a combination of some non-sensitive attribute values) [24] and/or one’s neighborhood information in the graph [38, 5].

Example 1

(Social-Network) Figure 1 is an example of a social-network graph before the anonymization and release. Each vertex in the graph corresponds to a user with two attributes, one non-sensitive attribute A1A_{1} and one sensitive attribute A2A_{2}. Here, for sensitive attribute A2A_{2} (e.g., salary), we assume that its value range is sensitive, if A2A_{2} is less than 0.2 (i.e., low salary). Each edge represents the friendship between two users.

From Figure 1, the release of such a graph may greatly threaten the privacy of users, for example, vertex v4v_{4} with low salary. Thus, it is very important to study how to release the most graph information (i.e., attribute values and graph structure), without revealing the users’ privacy.

In order to publish such social-network data while protecting the users’ privacy, one possible direction is to separately release the anonymized graph structure and users’ attribute values. For example, [38, 5] considered the graph structure attack only, and protected the users’ identities via any structure attack. As an example in Figure 1, by removing all attribute values at vertices, we can obtain a 2-automorphism anonymized graph [38], where each node cannot be distinguished from at least 1 (=2−1=2-1) other symmetric vertex via structural information. A better graph releasing strategy is to release both the graph structure and attribute values together. Yuan et al. [33] proposed a graph anonymization mechanism, called kk-degree-ll-diversity, which guarantees that the candidate set of any vertex has at least kk candidate vertices (i.e., kk-anonymity [24]) with the same degree and contains at least ll different values on sensitive attribute (i.e., ll-diversity [21]).

Example 2

(Privacy Disclosure) In Figure 1, vertices v1v_{1} and v4v_{4} satisfy the 2-degree-2-diversity requirement, where they both have 2 similar vertices (i.e., v1v_{1} and v4v_{4}) and contain 2 different values (i.e., 0.1 and 0.7) on the sensitive attribute. However, this is actually not safe for vertices v1v_{1} and v4v_{4} in Figure 1, if we consider their neighbors’ information. For instance, the neighbors of vertices v1v_{1} and v4v_{4} are {v2,v3,v4}\{v_{2},v_{3},v_{4}\} and {v1,v5,v6}\{v_{1},v_{5},v_{6}\}, with non-sensitive attribute values {0.4,0.5,0.5}\{0.4,0.5,0.5\} and {0.5,0.6,0.4}\{0.5,0.6,0.4\}, respectively. If an attacker knows neighbors of v1v_{1} and v4v_{4} (including their non-sensitive attributes), this attacker can uniquely identify v1v_{1} and v4v_{4}, which reveals the privacy information of v1v_{1} and v4v_{4}.

Therefore, most existing works (e.g., [25, 33, 38, 5]) usually protected the privacy of either the graph structure only or vertex attributes only. Their proposed techniques cannot be directly applied to the problem of privacy preservation of graph data, since graph data not only have sensitive attribute values, but also contain sensitive relationships (i.e., edges) among vertices in the graph structure. Meanwhile, although there are a few works (e.g., [23]) that consider both vertex attributes and the graph structure, they assumed that the attacker only knows direct neighbors of vertices (i.e., 1-hop neighbors), which cannot resist from attackers with nn-hop (n>1n>1) neighbor information.

In this paper, we will explore how to release both the graph structure and attributes of vertices, while preventing the users’ identities and sensitive attribute values from the leakage. To achieve this goal, there are two requirements on the released graph. First, to avoid the graph structure attack, we need to take into account the structure of nn-hop neighbors for any vertex in the graph. Moreover, we need to consider the intersection attack, raised by the possible combinations of nn-hop neighbor graph structure and vertex attributes (from either the target vertex or its neighbors). One straightforward solution for the intersection attack is to separately publish the anonymized graph structure and vertex attribute values, in which vertex IDs are not consistent in both anonymized parts. However, this method will directly destroy the relationship between the graph structure and vertex attributes. Instead, in this paper, we aim to publish both the graph structure and attribute values of each vertex, under the premise of protecting the graph privacy via either nn-hop neighborhood attack or attribute-related attack (e.g., quasi-identifier).

Specifically, in this paper, we will adopt kk-anonymity [24] and tt-closeness [18] (a stronger privacy mechanism than ll-diversity [21]) to guarantee the privacy preservation for vertex attributes in graph data. Furthermore, for the graph structure, we will protect the vertex identity from nn-hop neighbor attack by inserting fake nodes, edges, and/or attributes.

Example 3

(An Anonymized Graph) Figure 2 illustrates an anonymized graph of the social-network graph in Figure 1 by adding two fake vertices, v7v_{7} and v8v_{8}, with non-sensitive attribute values 0.6 and 0.5, as the new neighbors of vertices v1v_{1} and v4v_{4}, respectively. We can see that vertices v1v_{1} and v4v_{4} cannot be identified by an attacker through their neighbors’ information, since either v1v_{1} or v2v_{2} has 4 neighbors with the same set of non-sensitive attributes.

To tackle the graph privacy preservation problem, in this paper, we will formalize a novel graph privacy preservation mechanism, namely k​tkt-safe graph, which can efficiently anonymize the graph by letting their nn-hop neighbors contain the same or similar information (e.g., same/similar non-sensitive values). We prove that the k​tkt-safe graph generation is NP-hard and not tractable. Therefore, we propose a feasible framework for the k​tkt-safe graph anonymization, and optimize the framework by designing a cost-model-based graph partitioning strategy, proposing an effective pruning method, and devising a tree synopsis for facilitating efficient anonymization process (especially for a large-scale graph).

Note that, unlike previous works that release graph statistics only [7, 9] or synthetically generated (anonymized) graphs [12], in this paper, we aim to publish a “real” anonymized graph. Moreover, even if we use the widely adopted differential privacy mechanism [10, 9] to release a real anonymized graph (rather than graph statistics [9]), it may introduce too many nodes/edges in the real attributed graph due to its strong privacy guarantee, which leads to poor utility of the anonymized graph. We would like to leave interesting topics of releasing real attributed anonymized graphs via the differential privacy as our future work.

Contributions. In this paper, we make the following contributions:

  1. 1.

    We formalize a novel and important problem, namely kt-safety graph anonymization, based on our newly proposed graph privacy-preservation mechanism, kt-safety, in Section II.

  2. 2.

    We prove the NP-hardness of the kt-safety graph anonymization problem, and propose a feasible k​tkt-safe graph generation framework in Section III.

  3. 3.

    We propose the detailed algorithms, under our k​tkt-safe graph generation framework in Section IV.

  4. 4.

    We design a cost-model-based graph partitioning strategy, a pruning method, and a tree synopsis to optimize the k​tkt-safe graph anonymization process in Section V.

  5. 5.

    We evaluate through extensive experiments the performance of our k​tkt-safe graph generation approach on real/synthetic data in Section VI.

In addition, Section VII reviews related works on privacy preservation over tabular and graph data. Section VIII concludes this paper.

II Problem Definition

II-A Models

In this subsection, we present the graph model considered in this paper, and the model of the attacker’s knowledge used for identifying some target vertices.

Graph Model: First, we give the definition of graph data (e.g., social networks) as follows.

Definition 1

(Graph, GG) A graph GG is represented by a triple (V⁡(G),E⁡(G),A⁡(G))(V(G),E(G),A(G)). Here, V⁡(G)V(G) is a set of vertices (nodes) viv_{i} (for 1≤i≤|V⁡(G)|1\leq i\leq|V(G)|), E⁡(G)E(G) is a set of unlabelled edges eje_{j} (for 1≤j≤|E⁡(G)|1\leq j\leq|E(G)|), and A⁡(G)=(A1,…,Ad−1,Ad)A(G)=(A_{1},...,A_{d-1},A_{d}) is an attribute set at each vertex vi∈V⁡(G)v_{i}\in V(G), where the first (d−1)(d-1) attributes AjA_{j} (for 1≤j≤d−11\leq j\leq d-1) are non-sensitive attributes and the dd-th attribute AdA_{d} is a sensitive attribute.   \blacksquare\blacksquare

In Definition 1, we use vi.Ajv_{i}.A_{j} to denote the value of attribute AjA_{j} at vertex viv_{i}. When an attribute value vi.Ajv_{i}.A_{j} is not available (or missing), we denote it as vi.Aj=v_{i}.A_{j}=“-”. The first (d−1)(d-1) attributes, (vi.A1,…,vi.Ad−1)(v_{i}.A_{1},...,v_{i}.A_{d-1}), of each vertex viv_{i} can be used as a quasi-identifier, denoted as vi.Q​Iv_{i}.QI, which partially discloses the identity of vertex viv_{i}. Moreover, the dd-th attribute, vi.Adv_{i}.A_{d}, contains a sensitive value that the user (vertex) viv_{i} is not willing to disclose (e.g., user’s age, salary, home address, or mobile number).

For simplicity, in this paper, we assume that there is only one sensitive attribute for each vertex. Nonetheless, our graph model can be easily extended to multiple sensitive attributes to be anonymized, by treating these sensitive attributes as a composite attribute.

Attacker Model: An attacker who wants to uniquely identify a vertex in the graph (e.g., some user in a social-network graph) may have a priori knowledge about features of this vertex, which is defined as follows.

Definition 2

(Attacker Model) We assume that an attacker knows the quasi-identifier, vi.Q​Iv_{i}.QI, of a target vertex viv_{i} and its nn-hop neighbor information, denoted as H​N​(vi,n)HN(v_{i},n), where H​N​(vi,n)HN(v_{i},n) is a subgraph containing all neighbor vertices (with their non-sensitive attributes) that are less than or equal to nn hops away from viv_{i}.   \blacksquare\blacksquare

In Definition 2, an attacker can have two types of background information about a target vertex viv_{i}, which are the target’s quasi-identifier vi.Q​Iv_{i}.QI and its nn-hop neighbor information H​N​(vi,n)HN(v_{i},n) (i.e., a subgraph structure with nn-hop neighbors of viv_{i}, containing non-sensitive attributes). In a special case where n=0n=0, the attacker only knows the quasi-identifier of the target vertex viv_{i}.

II-B k​tkt-Safe Graph via Privacy Mechanisms

Preliminary: Prior privacy mechanisms such as kk-anonymity [24] and tt-closeness [18] are usually proposed for tabular data, which produce an anonymized version of the original tabular data. As a result, even if an attacker has the quasi-identifier of a target record, he/she can only obtain a set of candidate records, but still cannot uniquely identify the target from these records. Specifically, kk-anonymity requires the size of this candidate set not be smaller than kk, whereas tt-closeness requires the distribution of sensitive attribute values within this set be similar to that of the entire released data (i.e., distances between the two distributions should not be larger than a threshold tt).

Different from tabular data, the privacy protection over graph data is much more complex, since it involves the relationships (i.e., edges in the graph structure) among vertices in the graph (e.g., users in social networks).

The Protection Set of a Vertex: Specifically, for each vertex viv_{i} (associated with a quasi-identifier vi.Q​Iv_{i}.QI and its nn-hop neighbor information H​N​(vi,n)HN(v_{i},n)) in the privacy-preserved graph, we aim to guarantee that there exists a set, vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS, of (at least kk) candidate vertices vmv_{m} with the same quasi-identifier vm.Q​Iv_{m}.QI as vi.Q​Iv_{i}.QI and nn-hop neighbor information H​N​(vm,n)HN(v_{m},n) similar to H​N​(vi,n)HN(v_{i},n).

Below, we define the protection set, vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS, of vertex viv_{i}.

Definition 3

(Protection Set, vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS) Given a parameter tt, a graph edit distance threshold ϵ\epsilon, and a vertex viv_{i} with its quasi-identifier vi.Q​Iv_{i}.QI and nn-hop neighbor information H​N​(vi,n)HN(v_{i},n), a protection set, vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS, of vertex viv_{i} is a set of vertices vmv_{m} that satisfy the following three conditions:

  1. 1.

    vi.Q​I=vm.Q​Iv_{i}.QI=v_{m}.QI;

  2. 2.

    g​e​d​(H​N​(vi,n),H​N​(vm,n))≤ϵged(HN(v_{i},n),HN(v_{m},n))\leq\epsilon; and

  3. 3.

    a​t​t​_​d​i​s​t​(H​N​(vi,L),H​N​(vm,L),Aj)≤tatt\_dist(HN(v_{i},L),HN(v_{m},L),A_{j})\leq t (for 1≤j≤d−11\leq j\leq d-1 and 1≤L≤n1\leq L\leq n);

where g​e​d​(g1,g2)ged(g_{1},g_{2}) is the graph edit distance between subgraphs g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} by considering vertex/edge insertion operators, H​N​(vi,L)HN(v_{i},L) is a subgraph that contains all neighbor vertices that are less than or equal to LL hops away from viv_{i}, and a​t​t​_​d​i​s​t​(g1,g2,Aj)att\_dist(g_{1},g_{2},A_{j}) is a distance function between attribute value distributions from subgraphs g1g_{1} and g2g_{2}, for each non-sensitive attribute AjA_{j} (1≤j≤d−11\leq j\leq d-1).   \blacksquare\blacksquare

Intuitively, in Definition 3, the protection set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS contains a set of vertices vmv_{m} with (1) the same quasi-identifiers as vi.Q​Iv_{i}.QI, (2) graph structures of nn-hop neighbors similar to that of H​N​(vi,n)HN(v_{i},n) (restricted via parameters nn and ϵ\epsilon), and (3) non-sensitive attributes AjA_{j} in subgraphs H​N​(vm,L)HN(v_{m},L) similar to that of H​N​(vi,L)HN(v_{i},L) (restrained via parameter tt). Note that, we do not want to identify vertex viv_{i} from the distributions of non-sensitive attributes of its LL-hop neighbors H​N​(vi,L)HN(v_{i},L). Thus, in Definition 3, we apply tt-closeness [18] to the distributions of non-sensitive attributes AjA_{j}, which can indirectly protect sensitive attribute values of graph nodes.

To preserve the privacy of graph data, in this paper, we consider graph edit operators such as node and edge insertions. Therefore, the graph edit distance, g​e​d​(H​N​(vi,n)CLOSE,ged(HN(v_{i},n), OPENH​N​(vm,n))HN(v_{m},n)), is given by considering vertex or edge insertion operators (i.e., changes of the graph structure).

(1).

Goals of Graph Privacy Preservation: We want to release an anonymized (privacy-preserved) graph that prevents the privacy of any vertex viv_{i} from leakage, with the following two goals:

  1. 1.

    the attacker cannot uniquely link (identify) any vertex viv_{i} in graph GG to some vertices via quasi-identifier vi.Q​Iv_{i}.QI and nn-hop neighbor information H​N​(vi,n)HN(v_{i},n) with high confidences, and;

  2. 2.

    the attacker cannot deduce a vertex’s sensitive attributes to precise values via vi.Q​Iv_{i}.QI and H​N​(vi,n)HN(v_{i},n) with high confidences.

We define a safe (privacy-preserved) vertex as follows.

Definition 4

(k​tkt-Safe Vertex) Given thresholds kk, tt, α\alpha, and ϵ\epsilon, a vertex viv_{i} is k​tkt-safe, if it satisfies the two conditions below:

  1. 1.

    |vi.PS|≥k|v_{i}.PS|\geq k, and;

  2. 2.

    Ps​e​n​s(vi.PS,Ad)≤αP_{sens}(v_{i}.PS,A_{d})\leq\alpha,

where |⋅||\cdot| is the size of ⋅\cdot, and Ps​e​n​s(vi.PS,Ad)P_{sens}(v_{i}.PS,A_{d}) is the fraction of vertices vm∈vi.P​Sv_{m}\in v_{i}.PS that have sensitive values for sensitive attribute AdA_{d}.   \blacksquare\blacksquare

Intuitively, in Definition 4, a vertex viv_{i} is k​tkt-safe, if (1) viv_{i} has at least kk vertices, vmv_{m}, in the protection set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS, and (2) less than (100⋅α)%(100\cdot\alpha)\% of vertices vm∈vi.P​Sv_{m}\in v_{i}.PS have sensitive values for attribute AdA_{d}. Note that, here we consider attribute AdA_{d} having either sensitive or non-sensitive values. For example, for the disease attribute, its values like “AIDS” and “cancer” are sensitive, whereas attribute values such as “flu” and “cold” are not so sensitive. With the two conditions above, we cannot distinguish viv_{i} from other vertices in vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS and disclose sensitive attribute values. Thus, we call viv_{i} a k​tkt-safe vertex.

Definition 5

(k​tkt-Safe Graph) Given a graph GG and thresholds kk, tt, α\alpha, and ϵ\epsilon, we call the anonymized graph G′G^{\prime} of GG a k​tkt-safe graph, if any vertex vi∈V⁡(G′)v_{i}\in V(G^{\prime}) is k​tkt-safe.  \blacksquare\blacksquare

In Definition 5, given a graph GG, the anonymized graph G′G^{\prime} is k​tkt-safe, if all vertices vi∈V⁡(G′)v_{i}\in V(G^{\prime}) are k​tkt-safe (i.e., the privacy of every vertex in G′G^{\prime} is well preserved).

Discussions on the k​tkt-Safety Model: Our k​tkt-safety model adopts the kk-anonymity [24, 8] for the protection set (as given by Definition 4), and the tt-closeness for non-sensitive attributes in the protection set (as given by Definition 3). Essentially, our goal is to protect the identity and sensitive attribute values of each node viv_{i} in the graph.

Note that, our k​tkt-safety model can be easily extended to protecting both the identity and link safety, by setting neighbor-related parameters ϵ\epsilon and tt (given in Definition 3) to 0. Moreover, we can easily extend our k​tkt-safety model to other privacy mechanisms, for example, updating tt-closeness with β\beta-likeness [3], by revising the distance function from a​t​t​_​d​i​s​t​(H​N​(vi,L),H​N​(vm,L)CLOSE,att\_dist(HN(v_{i},L),HN(v_{m},L), OPENAj)A_{j}) to a​t​t​_​d​i​s​t​(H​N​(vi,L),H​N​(vm,L),aj)att\_dist(HN(v_{i},L),HN(v_{m},L),a_{j}), where aj∈d​o​m​(Aj)a_{j}\in dom(A_{j}) are the values on non-sensitive attributes AjA_{j}.

II-C k​tkt-Safe Graph Anonymization Problem

The Anonymization Cost: We define the cost of the graph anonymization as follows.

Definition 6

(The Anonymization Cost) Given a graph GG and its anonymized graph G′G^{\prime}, the anonymization cost, C​o​s​t​(G,G′)Cost(G,G^{\prime}), from GG to G′G^{\prime} is given by:

C​o​s​t​(G,G′)=|(V⁡(G′)∪V⁡(G))−(V⁡(G′)∩V⁡(G))|\displaystyle\hskip-8.61108ptCost(G,G^{\prime})=|(V(G^{\prime})\cup V(G))-(V(G^{\prime})\cap V(G))|
+|(E⁡(G′)∪E⁡(G))−(E⁡(G′)∩E⁡(G))|,\displaystyle+|(E(G^{\prime})\cup E(G))-(E(G^{\prime})\cap E(G))|, (2)

where V⁡(G)V(G) and E⁡(G)E(G) are the sets of nodes and edges in graph GG, respectively, and |S||S| is the size of set SS.  \blacksquare\blacksquare

In Definition 6, the anonymization cost, C​o​s​t​(G,G′)Cost(G,G^{\prime}), is defined as the total number of graph edit operators from GG to G′G^{\prime} (as given by Eq. (2)).

In particular, the first term in Eq. (2) (i.e., |(V⁡(G′)∪V⁡(G))−(V⁡(G′)∩V⁡(G))||(V(G^{\prime})\cup V(G))-(V(G^{\prime})\cap V(G))|) is the cost of vertex edits from GG to G′G^{\prime}, while the second term in Eq. (2) (i.e., |(E⁡(G′)∪E⁡(G))−(E⁡(G′)∩E⁡(G))||(E(G^{\prime})\cup E(G))-(E(G^{\prime})\cap E(G))|) corresponds to the cost of edge edits from GG to G′G^{\prime}. The anonymization cost C​o​s​t​(G,G′)Cost(G,G^{\prime}) sums up the two terms above.

Graph Release via kk-Anonymity and tt-Closeness: After defining the anonymization cost for graph privacy preservation, we provide the definition of our k​tkt-safe graph anonymization problem below.

Definition 7

(k​tkt-Safe Graph Anonymization Problem) Given a graph GG, and thresholds kk, tt, α\alpha, and ϵ\epsilon, the problem of k​tkt-safe graph anonymization is to produce an anonymized k​tkt-safe graph G′G^{\prime} from GG, with minimal anonymization cost C​o​s​t​(G,G′)Cost(G,G^{\prime}) (given in Eq. (2)).  \blacksquare\blacksquare

In Definition 7, given a graph GG, the k​tkt-safe graph anonymization problem aims to generate and release an anonymized k​tkt-safe graph G′G^{\prime} from graph GG with the minimum anonymization cost in Definition 6.

Challenges: The major challenges to tackle the k​tkt-safe graph anonymization problem are twofold. First, previous works assumed that an attacker knows the quasi-identifier and degree of a target only [33], or the graph structure of the target’s nn-hop neighbors only [38, 5]. However, this assumption may not always hold in practice, since the attacker may know both quasi-identifier and nn-hop neighbors (for n≥1n\geq 1, as given in Definition 2). It is non-trivial how to protect the identity and sensitive attribute values of each vertex against attacker’s knowledge in Definition 2. Thus, we need to propose an effective solution to transforming each vertex in GG to a k​tkt-safe vertex.

Second, it is very challenging to efficiently anonymizing vertices for the large-scale graph. The k​tkt-safe graph anonymization problem is NP-hard (as will be proved in Section III-A) and thus intractable. We need to design efficient heuristic approaches to improve the efficiency of the graph anonymization.

III k​tkt-safe graph Generation

III-A NP-hardness of the k​tkt-Safe Graph Anonymization Problem

Theorem III.1

(NP-hardness) The structural-attack-resistance-only version of k​tkt-safe graph anonymization problem in Definition 7 is NP-hard.

Proof: Please refer to Appendix A-A in our supplemental material.   \square\square

III-B k​tkt-Safe Graph Generation Framework

Since the k​tkt-safe graph anonymization problem is NP-hard and not tractable, we will propose alternative heuristics-based algorithms. Specifically, Algorithm 1 illustrates a heuristic-based k​tkt-safe graph generation framework, which produces a k​tkt-safe graph G′G^{\prime} from a given graph GG, where we only consider graph adding operations (i.e., inserting vertices/edges) for simplicity. We leave as our future work for extending Algorithm 1 by embedding graph deletion operations (i.e., removing vertices/edges).

This framework consists of three phases: preprocessing, k​tkt-safe graph generation, and k​tkt-safe graph merging phases. In the preprocessing phase, we first partition graph GG into ss disjoint subgraphs, and store these partitioned subgraphs in a set 𝒢\mathcal{G} via function p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n​_​g​r​a​p​h​(G,γ,s)partition\_graph(G,\gamma,s) (line 1).

In the k​tkt-safe graph generation phase, we make each partitioned subgraph g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G} a k​tkt-safe subgraph. For each partitioned subgraph gg in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, we sort vertices in gg in a queue QgQ_{g} by the counts of their (≤n)(\leq n)-hop neighbors in ascending order (line 4), based on which we anonymize vertices. Intuitively, the vertices with less neighbors should be considered first, since graph edit operators (i.e., insertion operators over vertex/edge/attribute) over these vertices may have less effect on the neighbor information of other unprocessed vertices. Next, for each vertex vi∈Qgv_{i}\in Q_{g} (assuming that viv_{i} is the target vertex), we invoke function i​n​i​t​i​a​l​_​c​a​n​d​i​d​a​t​e​(vi,g)initial\_candidate(v_{i},g), and retrieve an initial candidate set vi.C​Sv_{i}.CS for vi∈gv_{i}\in g (lines 5-6), which can be used for quickly obtaining the protection set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS of viv_{i}.

Then, for each vertex vi∈gv_{i}\in g in the queue QgQ_{g}, we make viv_{i} a k​tkt-safe vertex via function kt_safety_vertex(vi,vi.CS,g)kt\_safety\_vertex(v_{i},v_{i}.CS,g) (line 7). Note that, in the anonymization process of viv_{i}, if graph edit operators (i.e., adding edges/attributes) over a vertex vl∈gv_{l}\in g affects the privacy of previously anonymized vertices (i.e., identity or sensitive attribute values), then we will create a duplicate vl′v_{l}^{\prime} of vlv_{l}, and perform graph edits on duplicate vertex vl′v_{l}^{\prime} (instead of vlv_{l}). This way, we can obtain a k​tkt-safe graph g′g^{\prime} from subgraph g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G}, and add g′g^{\prime} to the set 𝒢′\mathcal{G^{\prime}} (lines 8-9).

In the k​tkt-safe graph merging phase, we merge vertices in k​tkt-safe subgraphs g′∈𝒢′g^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G^{\prime}} and their duplicates in other k​tkt-safe subgraphs in 𝒢′\mathcal{G^{\prime}} via function m​e​r​g​e​_​s​u​b​g​r​a​p​h​s​(𝒢′)merge\_subgraphs(\mathcal{G^{\prime}}) (line 10). Finally, we return the merged graph G′G^{\prime} as the k​tkt-safe graph (line 11).

Note that, Algorithm 1 can work for producing a k​tkt-safe anonymized graph without restricting the setup of nn-hop neighbors (i.e., n≥1n\geq 1). However, since exact GED calculation between two nn-hop neighbor subgraphs H​N​(v,n)HN(v,n) is an NP-hard problem for n>1n>1, the cost of GED computation for n>1n>1 is expected to be higher than that for n=1n=1. Moreover, we have an attack resistance discussion on the anonymized graph via Algorithm 1 (e.g., against minimality attack [29]). Please refer to Appendix A-C in the supplemental material for details.

IV Algorithms for k​tkt-safe graph Anonymization

Please refer to Appendix A-I in our supplemental material for a running example with the 3 phases of anonymizing the graph in Figure 1 via our k​tkt-safe graph generation approach.

IV-A Preprocessing Phase

Graph Partitioning: We use the divide-and-conquer strategy to divide GG into subgraphs with similar sizes, which reduces the time cost to anonymize each vertex to be k​tkt-safe by making each subgraph a k​tkt-safe graph.

Given a graph GG, the maximum size, γ\gamma, of subgraphs, and the number, ss, of partitions, we have an algorithm to produce a set, 𝒢\mathcal{G}, of partitioned subgraphs. Please refer to Algorithm 5 in Appendix A-D in our supplemental material for details.

Note that, after we divide GG into subgraphs gig_{i}, we will expand each subgraph gig_{i} by including duplicated nn-hop neighbors of border vertices v∈giv\in g_{i}. We will conduct the anonymization process on each expanded subgraph, and then merge the anonymized subgraphs.

Discussions on Parameters γ\gamma and ss. Please refer to Appendix A-E in our supplemental material for the discussions on parameters γ\gamma and ss.

IV-B k​tkt-Safe Graph Generation Phase

IV-B1 Candidate Set Detection

For any vertex viv_{i}, in order to obtain its protection set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS (as given in Definition 3), we will first retrieve its initial candidate set, vi.C​Sv_{i}.CS, of vertices vmv_{m} that satisfy the first two conditions (w.r.t. quasi-identifier and graph structure) in Definition 3, which we can further anonymize to obtain vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS (satisfying the third condition). Please refer to Algorithm 6 in Appendix A-F in our supplemental material for details.

Note that, if many vertices vm∈V⁡(G)v_{m}\in V(G) have the same quasi-identifier (i.e., vm.Q​Iv_{m}.QI) as viv_{i}, we will obtain many candidates in vi.C​Sv_{i}.CS, which leads to a lower anonymization cost to anonymize viv_{i} as a k​tkt-safe vertex later in Section IV-B2.

IV-B2 k​tkt-Safe Vertex Generation

Algorithm 2 illustrates the details of the k​tkt-safe graph generation phase, which obtains a protection set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS of each vertex viv_{i}, based on the candidate set vi.C​Sv_{i}.CS, and protects the identity and sensitive attribute values of viv_{i}, leveraging vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS.

Initialization of the Protection Set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS: In Algorithm 2, we first compute an initial protection set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS of vertex viv_{i} (based on the candidate set vi.C​Sv_{i}.CS) that satisfies the three conditions in Definition 3 (lines 1-11). Specifically, candidate vertices vmv_{m} in vi.C​Sv_{i}.CS satisfy the first two conditions of Definition 3. Thus, we only need to further check whether vertices vmv_{m} also satisfy the third condition (i.e., similar quasi-identifiers in LL-hop neighbors of vertex viv_{i}).

Specifically, for each vertex vm∈vi.C​Sv_{m}\in v_{i}.CS, we check the similarity of value distributions on attribute AjA_{j} (for 1≤j≤d−11\leq j\leq d-1) between LL-hop neighbors of viv_{i} and vmv_{m} (for 1≤L≤n1\leq L\leq n; lines 1-9). If it holds that a​t​t​_​d​i​s​t​(H​N​(vi,L),H​N​(vm,L),Aj)≤tatt\_dist(HN(v_{i},L),HN(v_{m},L),A_{j})\leq t for all non-sensitive attributes AjA_{j} (1≤j≤d−11\leq j\leq d-1) and all LL-hop neighbors (i.e., flag a​t​t​_​s​a​f​e=t​r​u​eatt\_safe=true holds), then we will add vmv_{m} to the protection set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS (lines 10-11).

Identity Protection of viv_{i}: After obtaining an initial protection set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS, we next aim to protect the identity of vertex viv_{i}, by letting |vi.PS|≥k|v_{i}.PS|\geq k hold (i.e., the first condition of the k​tkt-safe vertex in Definition 4).

Specifically, if the initial protection set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS satisfies the condition |vi.PS|≥k|v_{i}.PS|\geq k, then we do nothing; otherwise, we will let the remaining candidates in set (vi.CS−vi.PS)(v_{i}.CS-v_{i}.PS) become protection vertices for viv_{i} (lines 12-26). That is, when |vi.PS||v_{i}.PS| is less than kk, we will obtain Nn​e​e​d​e​dN_{needed} (=k−|vi.PS|)=k-|v_{i}.PS|) more vertices as protection vertices, either from (vi.CS−vi.PS)(v_{i}.CS-v_{i}.PS) (lines 14-23) and/or by adding fake duplicate nodes (lines 24-26).

For the remaining vertices vm∈(vi.CS−vi.PS)v_{m}\in(v_{i}.CS-v_{i}.PS) that do not satisfy the third condition (w.r.t. attribute distributions) in Definition 3, we will attempt to add new nodes (and edges as well) to their LL-hop neighbors to make them the members of vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS (i.e., vm∈vi.P​Sv_{m}\in v_{i}.PS). Specifically, we will do a rehearsal to add some fake nodes and edges to make vmv_{m} satisfy the third condition of Definition 3, where the addition operations are finally executed only if they will not make vmv_{m} violate the first two conditions of Definition 3. If we can transform vmv_{m} to a member of vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS, then we will add it to vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS and update those vertices vlv_{l} affected by node/edge insertions for vmv_{m}, via vertex/edge duplication (lines 17-23). In particular, the anonymization operations of vm∈(vi.CS−vi.PS)v_{m}\in(v_{i}.CS-v_{i}.PS) may affect the privacy (i.e., identity and sensitive attribute values) of those k​tkt-safe vertices vlv_{l}, prior to viv_{i} in the queue QGQ_{G}. Thus, in the case that graph edit operators on a vertex vav_{a} affect vlv_{l}, we will duplicate vav_{a} and obtain va′v_{a}^{\prime} to proceed the operators (lines 19-22). That is, the anonymization operations of a vertex do not affect the privacy of previously anonymized vertices. When we include a new vertex vm∈vi.P​Sv_{m}\in v_{i}.PS, we will decrease the variable Nn​e​e​d​e​dN_{needed} by 1 (line 23). The iteration process terminates, when Nn​e​e​d​e​d=0N_{needed}=0 holds (lines 15-16) or there are no more vertices in (vi.CS−vi.PS)(v_{i}.CS-v_{i}.PS) (line 14).

After checking all vertices in vi.C​Sv_{i}.CS, if we still need more vertices in the protection set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS (i.e., Nn​e​e​d​e​d>0N_{needed}>0), then we have to add Nn​e​e​d​e​dN_{needed} fake duplicate nodes vi′v_{i}^{\prime} of viv_{i} with non-sensitive values on attribute AdA_{d} and with the same associated edges as viv_{i} (lines 24-25). Then, we include duplicate nodes vi′v_{i}^{\prime} in the protection set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS (line 26).

Sensitive Attribute Value Protection of viv_{i}: Next, we will let vertex viv_{i} satisfy the second condition of the k​tkt-safe vertex in Definition 4 (i.e., Ps​e​n​s(vi.PS,Ad)≤αP_{sens}(v_{i}.PS,A_{d})\leq\alpha). Specifically, if it holds that Ps​e​n​s(vi.PS,Ad)>αP_{sens}(v_{i}.PS,A_{d})>\alpha, we will add to graph GG xx fake duplicates of existing vertices vm∈vi.P​Sv_{m}\in v_{i}.PS, but with different non-sensitive values on attribute AdA_{d}, where xx is given by ⌈Ns​e​n​sα−|vi.PS|⌉\left\lceil\frac{N_{sens}}{\alpha}-|v_{i}.PS|\right\rceil and Ns​e​n​sN_{sens} is the count of vertices vm∈vi.P​Sv_{m}\in v_{i}.PS with sensitive values on attribute AdA_{d} (line 28). Finally, we include these vertices vi′v_{i}^{\prime} in the protection set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS (line 29). This way, we can obtain a protection set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS for vertex viv_{i}, such that viv_{i} is a k​tkt-safe vertex (satisfying the two conditions in Definition 4).

Discussions on Parameters kk, tt, ϵ\epsilon and α\alpha. Please refer to Appendix A-G in our supplemental material for the discussions on parameters kk, tt, ϵ\epsilon and α\alpha.

IV-C k​tkt-Safe Graph Merging Phase

In the k​tkt-safe graph merging phase, Algorithm 3 merges the anonymized k​tkt-safe subgraphs from 𝒢′\mathcal{G^{\prime}} back to one single k​tkt-safe graph G′G^{\prime}. In particular, for any two (expanded) k​tkt-safe subgraphs, g1g_{1} and g2g_{2}, from 𝒢′\mathcal{G^{\prime}}, we need to merge the original vertices vv and their duplicates v′v^{\prime} (lines 1-6). That is, if H​N​(v,n)HN(v,n) and H​N​(v′,n)HN(v^{\prime},n) are not modified (compared with the original graph GG), then we can merge vv and v′v^{\prime} into the same vertex; otherwise, we will keep both versions (lines 3-6). This way, we can obtain a merged graph gg from g1g_{1} and g2g_{2}, and update the set 𝒢′\mathcal{G^{\prime}} (lines 7-8). Finally, there is only one graph G′G^{\prime} left in 𝒢′\mathcal{G}^{\prime}, which will be returned as the refined k​tkt-safe graph (line 9).

IV-D Complexity Analysis

In this subsection, we first provide the time complexity of k​tkt-safe graph anonymization algorithms. The graph partitioning (Algorithm 5 in Appendix A-D in our supplemental material) needs O⁡(|V⁡(G)|⋅l​o​g​(|V⁡(G)|))O(|V(G)|\cdot log(|V(G)|)) time complexity, which includes the cost to load vertices O⁡(|V⁡(G)|)O(|V(G)|) and that to assign vertices to ss subgraphs O⁡(|V⁡(G)|⋅l​o​g​(|V⁡(G)|))O(|V(G)|\cdot log(|V(G)|)). The candidate set detection (Algorithm 6 in Appendix A-F in our supplemental material) needs O⁡(|V⁡(G)|⋅Cn​-​h​o​p)O(|V(G)|\cdot C_{n\text{-}hop}) time complexity in the worst case (i.e., all vertices share the same quasi-identifiers), where Cn​-​h​o​pC_{n\text{-}hop} is the average time cost to calculate the graph edit distance between H​N​(vi,n)HN(v_{i},n) and H​N​(vm,n)HN(v_{m},n). The k​tkt-safe vertex anonymization (Algorithm 2) takes O(|vi.CS|⋅|V(G)|⋅(|V(G)|+E(G)|)+|vi.CS|α⋅(|V(G)|+|E(G)|))O(|v_{i}.CS|\cdot|V(G)|\cdot(|V(G)|+E(G)|)+\frac{|v_{i}.CS|}{\alpha}\cdot(|V(G)|+|E(G)|)) time complexity in the worst case, which contains 1) the cost to initialize the protection set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS of viv_{i} O(|vi.CS|⋅n⋅(d−1))O(|v_{i}.CS|\cdot n\cdot(d-1)) when the neighbors H​N​(vm,n)HN(v_{m},n) of all candidate vertices vm∈vi.C​Sv_{m}\in v_{i}.CS of viv_{i} have the similar value distribution on all non-sensitive attributes (lines 1-11), 2) the cost to make each vertex vm∈(vi.CS−vi.PS)v_{m}\in(v_{i}.CS-v_{i}.PS) a member of vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS O(|vi.CS|⋅|V(G)|⋅(|V(G)|+E(G)|))O(|v_{i}.CS|\cdot|V(G)|\cdot(|V(G)|+E(G)|)) when the anonymization of vm∈vi.C​Sv_{m}\in v_{i}.CS affects the privacy of all previous anonymized k​tkt-safe vertices (O⁡(|V⁡(G)|)O(|V(G)|)) and requires graph operations to be conducted over duplicated vertices (needing O(|V(G)|+E(G)|)O(|V(G)|+E(G)|)) (lines 14-23), 3) the cost to add fake vertices and make them as the members of vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS O⁡(k⋅(|V⁡(G)|+|E⁡(G)|))O(k\cdot(|V(G)|+|E(G)|)) when the vertices vm∈vi.C​Sv_{m}\in v_{i}.CS cannot be anonymized as members of vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS (lines 24-26), and 4) the cost to add extra fake vertices to meet the privacy requirement Ps​e​n​s(vi.PS,Ad)≤αP_{sens}(v_{i}.PS,A_{d})\leq\alpha and anonymize these fake vertices as members of vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS O⁡(|vi.CS|α⋅(|V⁡(G)|+|E⁡(G)|))O(\frac{|v_{i}.CS|}{\alpha}\cdot(|V(G)|+|E(G)|)) when all vertices vm∈vi.C​Sv_{m}\in v_{i}.CS can be anonymized as members of vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS but all vmv_{m} hold sensitive values on attribute AdA_{d}. The subgraph merging (Algorithm 3) requires O(|𝒢′|2⋅|g′|)O(|\mathcal{G^{\prime}}|^{2}\cdot|g^{{}^{\prime}}|) time complexity, where |𝒢′||\mathcal{G^{\prime}}| is the number of anonymized subgraphs g′g^{{}^{\prime}} in set 𝒢′\mathcal{G^{\prime}}, and |g′||g^{{}^{\prime}}| is the size of vertices in a subgraph g′g^{{}^{\prime}}.

For the anonymization cost (as given in Definition 6), our proposed k​tkt-safety anonymization algorithms need to add O⁡((k−1)⋅(|V⁡(G)|+|E⁡(G)|)⋅∏j=1d−1|d​o​m​(Aj)|)O((k-1)\cdot(|V(G)|+|E(G)|)\cdot\prod_{j=1}^{d-1}|dom(A_{j})|) nodes and/or edges in the worst case, when each node has a unique value on each non-sensitive attribute AjA_{j} (1≤j≤d−11\leq j\leq d-1), where |d​o​m​(Aj)||dom(A_{j})| is the domian size of attribute AjA_{j}. However, via the empirical evaluation of our anonymization algorithm over real/synthetic graphs, this anonymization cost is usually smaller than O⁡((k−1)⋅(|V⁡(G)|+|E⁡(G)|)CLOSEO((k-1)\cdot(|V(G)|+|E(G)|). Please refer to Section VI-D and Appendix C-D in our supplemental material for the anonymization cost evaluation.

V Optimizations for the k​tkt-safe graph Anonymization

In this section, we propose optimization techniques for improving the effectiveness and efficiency of k​tkt-safe graph anonymization algorithms. Specifically, we design a cost model to guide the graph partitioning in Section V-A, propose effective pruning strategies to accelerate the candidate set retrieval for each vertex in Section V-B, and devise a tree synopsis to facilitate efficient anonymization of a graph GG in Section V-C.

V-A Cost Model for Graph Partitioning

In the preprocessing phase in Section IV-A, we need to partition graph GG into disjoint subgraphs of similar sizes. Since the anonymization cost highly depends on the graph partitioning strategy, in this subsection, we will propose a cost model to estimate the anonymizaiton cost of a graph partitioning strategy 𝒢′\mathcal{G^{\prime}}, and guide the graph partitioning process.

The basic idea of our cost model is as follows. We retrieve a (small) sample graph SS from GG, and anonymize SS as a k​tkt-safe graph S′S^{{}^{\prime}} via our proposed approach (Algorithm 1). The total cost of anonymizing SS comes from two parts, anonymization and merging. For anonymization cost, it is the sum of anonymization cost u.Cm​k​tu.C_{mkt} for making each vertex u∈Su\in S to be k​tkt-safe. For merging cost, it equals to the sum of cost u′.Cm​e​ru^{{}^{\prime}}.C_{mer} for merging each border vertex u′∈Su^{{}^{\prime}}\in S and its duplicates. Then, given a graph partitioning strategy, we estimate the anonymization cost C​o​s​t​(G,G′)Cost(G,G^{\prime}) of GG in Eq. (2), by summing up the approximate cost of each vertex v∈𝒢v\in\mathcal{G} to be k​tkt-safe and that of each border vertex v′∈𝒢v^{{}^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{G} to be merged based on the sample SS. Specifically, we estimate the anonymization cost, C​o​s​t​(G,G′)Cost(G,G^{\prime}), below.

C​o​s​t​(G,G′)\displaystyle Cost(G,G^{\prime}) (3)
=\displaystyle= C​o​s​ta​n​o​n​y​m​i​z​a​t​i​o​n+C​o​s​tm​e​r​g​i​n​g\displaystyle Cost_{anonymization}+Cost_{merging}
=\displaystyle= ∑∀gi∈𝒢∑∀v∈gi{u.Cm​k​t|argminu∑∀u∈Sϑ(u,v,n)}\displaystyle\sum_{\forall g_{i}\in\mathcal{G}}\sum_{\forall v\in g_{i}}\{u.C_{mkt}|arg\min\limits_{u}\sum_{\forall u\in S}\vartheta(u,v,n)\}
+∑∀gi∈𝒢,gh∈𝒢⁡(i≠h)∑∀v′∈gi∪gh{u′.Cm​e​r|argminu′∑∀u′∈Sϑ(u′,v′,n)},\displaystyle+\hskip-21.52771pt\sum_{\forall g_{i}\in\mathcal{G},g_{h}\in\mathcal{G}(i\neq h)}\sum_{\forall v^{{}^{\prime}}\in g_{i}\cup g_{h}}\hskip-8.61108pt\{u^{{}^{\prime}}.C_{mer}|arg\min\limits_{u^{{}^{\prime}}}\sum_{\forall u^{{}^{\prime}}\in S}\vartheta(u^{{}^{\prime}},v^{{}^{\prime}},n)\},

where SS is a sample graph from GG containing vertices uu, u.Cm​k​tu.C_{mkt} is the anonymization cost of sample uu to be k​tkt-safe, u′.Cm​e​ru^{{}^{\prime}}.C_{mer} is the cost of border vertices u′u^{{}^{\prime}} and their duplicates to be merged, and function ϑ⁡(u,v,n)\vartheta(u,v,n)==|V⁡(H​N​(u,n))|−|V⁡(H​N​(v,n))||V(HN(u,n))|-|V(HN(v,n))| calculates the difference of vertex numbers from subgraphs H​N​(u,n)HN(u,n) and H​N​(v,n)HN(v,n).

For each subgraph gi⊆𝒢g_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{G}, based on the processing order QgiQ_{g_{i}}, we estimate the k​tkt-safety cost of each vertex v∈giv\in g_{i} as the cost u.Cm​k​tu.C_{mkt} of sample u∈Su\in S to be k​tkt-safe, where uu is the most similar sample to vv among all samples in SS w.r.t. their nn-hop neighbor size (i.e., u=a​r​g​min⁡∑∀u∈Su⁡ϑ⁡(u,v,n)u=arg\min\limits_{u}\sum_{\forall u\in S}\vartheta(u,v,n)). Similarly, for each border vertex v′v^{{}^{\prime}} in any two subgraphs gig_{i} and ghg_{h}, we estimate its merging cost via the cost u′.Cm​e​ru^{{}^{\prime}}.C_{mer} of the most similar border sample u′u^{{}^{\prime}} to v′v^{{}^{\prime}} in SS to be merged.

Therefore, given a graph partitioning set 𝒢\mathcal{G}, we can use Eq. (3) to estimate the anonymization cost (i.e., Eq. (2)). Intuitively, a good partitioning set will have a low estimated anonymization cost via Eq. (3). We can also adopt existing graph partitioning approaches (e.g., [28]) to accelerate the graph anonymization, as long as the estimated anonymization cost via Eq. (3) remains low.

Cost-Model-Based Graph Partitioning. Given a graph GG, thresholds γ\gamma and ss, and an iteration i​t​eite, we have Algorithm 4 to select a good graph partitioning set 𝒢\mathcal{G}, based on the cost model in Eq. (3) (lines 1-14). Specifically, in the first iteration (i.e., i=1i=1), we randomly and recursively select |𝒢||\mathcal{G}| (determined by parameters γ\gamma and ss) centers, c​t​scts, from GG, and we obtain |𝒢||\mathcal{G}| subgraphs via clustering, in which cluster nodes in GG have the shortest path to a center in c​t​scts (lines 2-4). Note that, if the size of a subgraph reaches γ\gamma, we will not assign more vertices to this subgraph. Then, we use Eq. (3) to estimate the anonymization cost for anonymizing and merging subgraphs in 𝒢\mathcal{G} (line 5). In the remaining iterations (i.e., i≠1i\neq 1), we obtain a new set, C​T​sCTs, of centers (i.e., vertices) by randomly replacing a vertex in c​t​scts, obtain a new subgraph set 𝒢n​e​w\mathcal{G}_{new} based on centers in C​T​sCTs, and estimate the anonymization cost of the set 𝒢n​e​w\mathcal{G}_{new} via Eq. (3) (lines 6-9). We choose the partitioning set (either 𝒢\mathcal{G} or 𝒢n​e​w\mathcal{G}_{new}) with lower cost (lines 10-13). Finally, we return the set 𝒢\mathcal{G} with the minimal cost from i​t​eite iterations (line 14).

V-B Pruning Strategy

In the candidate set detection phase in Section IV-B1 (i.e., Algorithm 6 in Appendix A-F of our supplemental material), given a vertex vi∈V⁡(G)v_{i}\in V(G), in order to obtain its candidate set vi.C​Sv_{i}.CS, we need to compute the graph edit distance g​e​d​(H​N​(vi,n),H​N​(vm,n))ged(HN(v_{i},n),HN(v_{m},n)) between nn-hop neighbors of viv_{i} and each vertex vm∈V⁡(G)v_{m}\in V(G), which is rather costly. Assume that there is a vertex vpv_{p} whose nn-hop neighbors H​N​(vp,n)HN(v_{p},n) can be used as a pivot subgraph. Then, we can reduce the distance computation cost above via the triangle inequality by utilizing the pivot subgraph H​N​(vp,n)HN(v_{p},n) to filter out those vertices vmv_{m} that cannot be in the candidate set vi.C​Sv_{i}.CS.

The Pruning via Pivots. We have the pruning lemma below to rule out vertices vm∈Gv_{m}\in G whose nn-hop neighbor subgraphs are dissimilar to H​N​(vi,n)HN(v_{i},n).

Lemma V.1

(Pivot Pruning) Given two vertex nn-hop neighbor subgraphs H​N​(vi,n)HN(v_{i},n) and H​N​(vm,n)HN(v_{m},n), and a pivot nn-hop neighbor subgraph H​N​(vp,n)HN(v_{p},n), vertex vmv_{m} can be safely pruned (i.e., vm∉vi.C​Sv_{m}\notin v_{i}.CS), if it holds that |g​e​d​(H​N​(vi,n),H​N​(vp,n))−g​e​d​(H​N​(vm,n),H​N​(vp,n))|>ϵ|ged(HN(v_{i},n),HN(v_{p},n))-ged(HN(v_{m},n),HN(v_{p},n))|>\epsilon.

Proof: Please refer to Appendix A-B in the supplemental material.   \square\square

In practice, we can select a set, P​V​T​sPVTs, of pivots vp∈Gv_{p}\in G whose nn-hop neighbor subgraphs H​N​(vp,n)HN(v_{p},n) can be adopted to enable the pivot pruning (as discussed in Lemma V.1). If vmv_{m} can be pruned via any pivot vp∈P​V​T​sv_{p}\in PVTs, then vmv_{m} is not a candidate of the set vi.C​Sv_{i}.CS. Please refer to Appendix A-H in our supplemental material for the details of our pivot set selection strategy.

V-C k​tkt-Tree

Based on the selected pivot set P​V​T​sPVTs (via Algorithm 7 in Appendix A-H in our supplemental material), we propose a tree synopsis, k​tkt-tree (k​t​TktT), to further accelerate the retrieval process of candidates in vi.C​Sv_{i}.CS for each vertex vi∈Gv_{i}\in G.

k​tkt-Tree Synopsis. The k​tkt-tree, k​t​TktT, is a tree index built over graph GG, where each non-leaf node NN contains mm children nodes NiN_{i} (for 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m), and each child node NiN_{i} exclusively includes around (1/m×100)%(1/m\times 100)\% similar vertices in NN. Specifically, each leaf node in k​t​TktT includes vertices v∈Gv\in G with the same or similar quasi-identifiers. Moreover, we use a hash function, f(v.Aj)f(v.A_{j}), to hash value v.Ajv.A_{j} of a vertex v∈Gv\in G on non-sensitive attributes AjA_{j} (for 1≤j≤d−11\leq j\leq d-1) into a position in a bit vector with size BB, where B>1B>1 is an integer value. Each node N∈k​t​TN\in ktT contains two information:

  1. 1.

    (d−1)(d-1) bit vectors, Aj.v​e​cA_{j}.vec, obtained via bit OR operators over all hash bit values of v.Ajv.A_{j} of vertex v∈Nv\in N; and

  2. 2.

    a distance interval, p​v​t.Ipvt.I, of nn-hop neighbor subgraphs between vertices in NN and tree node (pivot) NN.

Index Construction. We build the k​tkt-tree index, k​t​TktT, by clustering vertices vv in GG in a bottom-up strategy. First, we cluster all vertices v∈Gv\in G based on their quasi-identifier v.Q​Iv.QI, and treat these clusters as the leaf nodes of k​t​TktT. For each leaf node including vertices vv with the same quasi-identifiers, we can get (d−1)(d-1) vectors Aj.v​e​cA_{j}.vec via hash function f(v.Aj)f(v.A_{j}). Given |P​V​T​s||PVTs| pivots p​v​tpvt obtained from Algorithm 7, we can group leaf nodes (containing vertices with the same quasi-identifier) into |P​V​T​s||PVTs| parent nodes via clustering, based on the graph edit distance between nn-hop neighbor subgraphs of vertices vv and pivots p​i​vpiv. Furthermore, we select |P​V​T​s|\sqrt{|PVTs|} pivots from the |P​V​T​s||PVTs| nodes, and cluster these nodes into |P​V​T​s|\sqrt{|PVTs|} supernodes with similar sizes. This process terminates until we reach the root of the k​t​TktT.

After we build the k​t​TktT, for each node in k​t​TktT, we calculate its stored information (i.e., Aj.v​e​cA_{j}.vec and p​v​t.Ipvt.I).

Vertex Pruning via k​t​TktT. With the k​t​TktT, for each vertex v∈Gv\in G, when we retrieve its candidate set v.C​Sv.CS, we can prune vertices v′v^{{}^{\prime}} in the leaf nodes N∈k​t​TN\in ktT that cannot contain the same quasi-identifier v′.QIv^{{}^{\prime}}.QI as v.Q​Iv.QI, where bit and operators over the (d−1)(d-1) vectors Aj.v​e​cA_{j}.vec of vv and NN return false. For vertices v′v^{{}^{\prime}} in the un-pruned leaf nodes N∈k​t​TN\in ktT, we calculate the graph edit distance between the nn-hop neighbor subgraph of vertex vv and pivot p​v​tpvt (of node NN), and then check whether or not v′v^{\prime} can be pruned via the pivot p​v​tpvt and the correspondingly stored distance interval p​v​t.Ipvt.I of node NN (Lemma V.1).

VI Experimental Evaluation

VI-A Experimental Settings

Real/Synthetic Data Sets. We evaluate the performance of our k​tkt-safety approach on 6 real and 3 synthetic data sets, as depicted in Table II. Please refer to Appendix B in our supplemental material for the detailed description of these tested data sets.

Competitors. We compare our k​tkt-safe graph generation approach, denoted as p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning, with four baseline approaches, namely k​l​-​g​r​a​p​hkl\text{-}graph, p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​npartition, p​r​u​n​i​n​gpruning, and n​o​n​enone, where p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning is our approach that applies both graph partition and pruning strategies (n=1n=1 by default), k​l​-​g​r​a​p​hkl\text{-}graph uses an existing kk-degree-ll-diversity [33] graph mechanism (l=2l=2 by default), p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​npartition considers our proposed graph partitioning approach only, p​r​u​n​i​n​gpruning uses our proposed pruning strategy only, and n​o​n​enone do not leverage any optimization method.

Measures. Following the literature [38], we report the distributions of three graph utility measures: vertex degrees, shortest path lengths, cluster coefficient. Specifically, the vertex degree distribution is the distribution of all vertices in graph; the shortest path length distribution is the distribution of the shortest path lengths between 1,000 randomly selected vertex pairs; and the cluster coefficient, also known as transitivity, is to measure the ratio of connected 11-hop neighbor pairs of a vertex among all 11-hop neighbor pairs of the vertex. Moreover, we report the mean and standard derivation of vertex degrees and shortest path length among 1,000 randomly selected vertices and vertex pairs, resp. Furthermore, we evaluate and report the sizes of largest components in the anonymized graphs. In addition, We evaluate the percentage of k​tkt-safety anonymized nodes after applying the kk-degree-ll-diversity [33]. Finally, we report the wall clock time (i.e., CPU time) and anonymization cost to anonymize a graph as k​tkt-safety.

Parameter Settings. Table III depicts experimental settings, where default values are in bold. We run our experiments on a PC with Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-6600U CPU 2.70 GHz and 32 GB memory. All algorithms were implemented by C++. The code is available at http://www.cs.kent.edu/~wren/kt-safety/.

VI-B Utility Evaluation

Due to space limitations, we report the utility result of our k​tkt-safe graph generation approach on E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions in this section and put the results of other 8 data sets to Appendix C-B in our supplemental material. In order to improve readability, we only report the utility evaluation results of the approaches p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning and p​r​u​n​i​n​gpruning, since the anonymized graphs via p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning and p​r​u​n​i​n​gpruning have the same utility performance as that of p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​npartition and n​o​n​enone, resp.

Utility Evaluation vs. Vertex Degree Distribution. Figure 3(a) evaluates the degree distributions of our proposed k​tkt-safe graph generation approach over E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions. Specifically, we illustrates the degree distribution of the original graph, which can be regarded as a standard. In figures, we can see that the generated k​tkt-safe graphs by our methods (including the 3 variants) vividly reveal the degree distribution trend of original graph. Moreover, from figures, p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning and p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​npartition add more fake nodes in the anonymization process than p​r​u​n​i​n​gpruning and n​o​n​enone, since they need more fake nodes to make each partitioned subgraph as k​tkt-safe.

Utility Evaluation vs. Shortest Path Length Distribution. Figure 3(b) demonstrates the distributions of shortest path lengths among 1,000 randomly selected vertex pairs over E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions. From figures, all the four approaches perform well for revealing the shortest path length distribution of the unanonymized graph. This is reasonable, since we only consider addition operations in graphs.

Please refer to Appendix C-B in our supplemental material for the evaluation of distributions of cluster coefficient, the mean and standard derivation of degrees and shortest path length among 1,000 randomly selected vertices and vertex pairs resp., and the largest component size over real/synthetic data.

VI-C Comparisons of Privacy Preservation Power

Table IV depicts the percentage of k​tkt-safety anonymized nodes after applying k​lkl-graph technique [33]. From the results, we can see that the anonymized graphs via k​l​-​g​r​a​p​hkl\text{-}graph cannot fully satisfy our k​t​-​s​a​f​e​t​ykt\text{-}safety requirement, since k​l​-​g​r​a​p​hkl\text{-}graph does not consider the intersection attack between quasi-identifiers (from both nodes and their neighbors) and graph structure. Note that, for an anonymized node via our k​t​-​s​a​f​e​t​ykt\text{-}safety approach, we cannot guarantee that it has at least kk candidates with the same degrees. However, since we do not lease the statistics of graph edit operators, the attackers cannot uniquely identify any target vertex and its sensitive attributes. Thus, k​t​-​s​a​f​e​t​ykt\text{-}safety is a better, feasible graph privacy mechanism (with stronger privacy preservation power) than k​l​-​g​r​a​p​hkl\text{-}graph for attributed graphs.

VI-D Efficiency Evaluation

Similar to utility evaluation, we only report the time and anonymization cost on C​o​r​aCora, D​B​L​PDBLP and E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions, and put the result on the other 6 graphs to Appendix C-C in our supplemental material.

Efficiency Evaluation vs. Data Sets. Figure 4(a) illustrates the wall clock time of anonymizing the graph for C​o​r​aCora, D​B​L​PDBLP, and E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions. From the figure, we can see that our approach, p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning, can achieve the lowest wall clock time on D​B​L​PDBLP and E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions, which indicates the efficiency of our graph anonymization approach. Note that, p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning needs more time cost than p​r​u​n​i​n​gpruning on C​o​r​aCora, since it needs to partition graph into subgraphs prior to the k​tkt-safe anonymization process. This indicates that we may not need to partition graphs in the preprocessing phase for small graphs, by setting the subgraph size threshold γ\gamma as a large value. For the three variants of our methods, p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​npartition (via divide-and-conquer) has the smallest wall clock time, which indicates the necessity of graph partitioning, especially for large graphs. Moreover, n​o​n​enone is expected to perform the worst. Please refer to Appendix C-C in our supplemental material for the break-up cost analysis of p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning on C​o​r​aCora, D​B​L​PDBLP, and E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions.

Anonymization Cost Evaluation. Figure 4(b) illustrates the anonymization cost of all the approaches on C​o​r​aCora, D​B​L​PDBLP and E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions. From the figure, p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning and p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​npartition have slightly higher cost than p​r​u​n​i​n​gpruning and n​o​n​enone, since they need to add more fake nodes to the partitioned subgraphs than that of the original single graph. However, our approach requires lower time cost for anonymizing large graphs (as shown in Figure 4(a)). Therefore, p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning can be used for anonymizing large graphs (e.g., D​B​L​PDBLP), whereas p​r​u​n​i​n​gpruning can be adopted over small graphs (e.g., C​o​r​aCora).

Time and Anonymization Cost Evaluation vs. the size, |Q​I||QI|, of vertices’ quasi-identifiers. Figure 5 reports the performance of our p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning approach on three synthetic data sets, by varying |Q​I||QI| from 10 to 100, where other parameters are set to their default values in Table III. From the figures, we can see that larger |Q​I||QI| leads to both higher time and anonymization costs. This is reasonable, since larger |Q​I||QI| will generate a more complex (stricter) neighborhood environment for each vertex to be anonymized. Therefore, for each vertex, we need more time to check its nn-hop neighborhood and add more fake nodes to make each vertex k​tkt-safe.

Time and Anonymization Cost Evaluation vs. nn. Figure 6 demonstrates the effect of the parameter nn on our P​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gPartition+pruning approach on C​o​r​aCora, D​B​L​PDBLP, and E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions, where n=n= 1 and 2, and other parameters are by default. From the figures, when nn increases, both time and anonymization costs increase, since we need to consider a larger range of neighborhood information for each vertex. Specifically, as shown in Figure 6(a), when nn changes from 1 to 2, the wall clock time of our approach increases by 1 order of magnitude (due to the NP-hardness of computing the GED between subgraphs). In Figure 6(b), the anonymization cost via our approach slightly increases for larger nn.

We also evaluated our p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning approach by systematically varying other parameters in Table III. Due to space limitations, we will not report similar experimental results here. For interested readers, please refer to Appendix C in our supplemental material for more efficiency and anonymization cost evaluations.

VII Related Work

Privacy Preservation for Tabular Data. The kk-anonymity [24] mechanism was first proposed to study the privacy issue of the released tabular table. In particular, it requires that any tuple tt in the released tabular table have a candidate set t.C​St.CS containing at least kk indistinguishable candidate records. After that, many works with various privacy preservation constraints have been proposed, including ll-diversity [21], tt-closeness [18], δ\delta-presence [22], mm-invariance [30], β\beta-likeness [3], differential privacy [9], and so on.

Differential privacy (DP) [9] is a more rigorous privacy preservation mechanism, requiring the inference probability of the presence of any element in a data set should be smaller than e​x​p​(ϵ)exp(\epsilon), where ϵ∈[0,1]\epsilon\in[0,1] is a privacy indicator. There are many existing works of the DP variant (e.g., [14]) and applications (e.g., [19, 6, 35, 32]).

Our work focuses on the privacy preservation over graph data (instead of tabular tables), which contain both vertex attributes and graph structures. We cannot directly borrow previous techniques for tabular data, due to the privacy preservation with graph structures.

Privacy Preservation for Graph Data. Existing works on the graph privacy can be classified into two categories: the ones applying the differential privacy (e.g., [4, 7, 12, 10, 13, 31]) and those adopting other privacy mechanisms like kk-anonymity (e.g., [38, 5, 2, 20, 34, 33, 36]). Moreover, there are some works (e.g., [1, 11]) studying possible attacker models for anonymized graphs.

Graph privacy via differential privacy. Hay et al. [10] first applied the differential privacy on graph data, and proposed two privacy-preservation mechanisms, edge-based and node-based differential privacies, which require the presence of any edge (e.g., relationship) and node (e.g., person) not be disclosed with high inferred confidences, respectively. Then, related works on differential privacy over graphs have two directions: publishing graph statistics (e.g., degree distribution [7]) and publishing the entire graph [10, 13, 31, 4, 12].

Although differential privacy is a very robust privacy mechanism (e.g., future proofed), it may not be a good choice for an attributed graph under our attacker model (Definition 2), which is the intersection of quasi-identifiers and nn-hop neighbors (including graph structure and their quasi-identifiers). Therefore, we do not consider differential privacy as a competitor/baseline in our experiments.

Graph privacy via other privacy mechanisms. Other existing works (e.g., [38, 5, 2, 20, 34, 33, 36, 23]) mainly leveraged the idea of kk-anonymity [24]. Specifically, Song et al. [23] proposed ll-sensitive-label-diversity mechanism, for protecting from 1-hop neighborhood attack, but cannot resist from an attacker with nn-hop (n>1n>1) neighbor information, which is the focus of our work.

Prior works mainly focused on the graph structure attack only (i.e., nn-hop neighbor attack) [38, 5]. Although some existing works [34, 33, 23] studied both 1-hop neighbors and attribute attacks (i.e., quasi-identifier of a vertex), they cannot protect the graph privacy if an attacker knows the vertex’s nn-hop (n>1n>1) neighbor information (containing both structural and quasi-identifier information). Thus, their proposed techniques cannot be directly applied to our k​tkt-safe graph anonymization problem.

VIII Conclusions

In this paper, we formalize an important problem, kt-safety graph anonymization, which is useful for protecting the privacy of the released graph data, in many real-world applications such as social networks, communication networks, citation networks, and so on. Due to the NP-hardness of the kt-safety graph anonymization problem, we propose a k​tkt-safe graph generation framework, which adopts the idea of divide-and-conquer to anonymize the graph data. In order to optimize the generation process of the k​tkt-safe graph, we design a cost-model-based graph partitioning strategy, and derive effective pruning and indexing mechanisms to improve the anonymization efficiency. Through extensive experiments on real/synthetic data, we confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed k​tkt-safe graph generation approach.

Appendix A More Technical Details

A-A Proof of Theorem III.1

Proof: We introduce a special instance of the k​tkt-safe graph anonymization problem in Definition 7 that resists from any structural attacks but ignores attribute-related attacks. We illustrate that this special instance itself is NP-hard, which can in turn prove the NP-hardness of the k​tkt-safe graph anonymization problem in Definition 7. Specifically, we prove the NP-hardness of the structural-attack-resistance-only instance by reducing from the kk-automorphism problem [38] which is an NP-hard problem. We provide a 4-step detailed proof as follows.

The kk-automorphism problem (Step 1). We give an instance of the kk-automorphism problem which takes a non-attributed graph GG and a parameter kk as input and aims to construct an anonymized graph G′G^{\prime} via graph edits with the minimal cost C​o​s​t​(G,G′)Cost(G,G^{\prime}). As a result, for each vertex vi∈G′v_{i}\in G^{\prime}, there exist (k−1)(k-1) automorphic functions Fa​(⋅)F_{a}(\cdot) (1≤a≤k−11\leq a\leq k-1), where Fa​(vi)F_{a}(v_{i}) returns a different vertex vi′v_{i}^{\prime} with exactly the same nn-hop neighborhood structure as that of the vertex viv_{i} and Fa​1​(vi)≠Fa​2​(vi)F_{a1}(v_{i})\neq F_{a2}(v_{i}) (a​1≠a​2a1\neq a2). That is, the anonymized graph G′G^{\prime} can protect its vertices from any (nn-hop) structural attack.

The structural-attack-resistance-only instance of the k​tkt-safe graph anonymization problem (Step 2). Given a non-attributed graph G=(V⁡(G),E⁡(G))G=(V(G),E(G)), and thresholds kk, t=1t=1, ϵ=0\epsilon=0, and α=1\alpha=1, the problem of the structural-attack-resistance-only instance of the k​tkt-safe graph anonymization problem is to produce an anonymized k​tkt-safe graph G′G^{\prime} from GG, with minimal anonymization cost C​o​s​t​(G,G′)Cost(G,G^{\prime}) (given by Eq. (2)).

The setup of graph model and thresholds (Step 3). There are two features for the instance of anonymized k​tkt-safe graph above. First, we simplify our graph model in Definition 1 from attributed graphs G=(V⁡(G),E⁡(G),A⁡(G))G=(V(G),E(G),A(G)) to non-attributed ones G=(V⁡(G),E⁡(G))G=(V(G),E(G)) by removing the set of vertices’ attributes (or equivalently setting them to the same value), and set attribute-related thresholds t=1t=1 and α=1\alpha=1. As a result, the conditions vi.Q​I=vm.Q​Iv_{i}.QI=v_{m}.QI and a​t​t​_​d​i​s​t​(H​N​(vi,L),H​N​(vm,L),Aj)≤tatt\_dist(HN(v_{i},L),HN(v_{m},L),A_{j})\leq t in Definition 3 and Ps​e​n​s(vi.PS,Ad)≤αP_{sens}(v_{i}.PS,A_{d})\leq\alpha in Definition 4 will always hold. Moreover, we strengthen the resistance of the anonymized k​tkt-safe graph from any (nn-hop) structural attacks, by setting ϵ=0\epsilon=0.

Reduction from the instance of the kk-automorphism problem to the structural-attack-resistance-only instance of the k​tkt-safe anonymization problem (Step 4). Given a non-attribute graph GG and a parameter kk as input, we can reduce the instance of the kk-automorphism problem to the structural-attack-resistance-only instance of the k​tkt-safe anonymization problem, by replacing the requirement of (k−1)(k-1) automorphic functions FaF_{a} for each vertex viv_{i} with the functionally equivalent limits of a k​tkt-safe vertex (|vi.PS|≥k|v_{i}.PS|\geq k and g​e​d​(H​N​(vi,n),H​N​(vm,n))=0ged(HN(v_{i},n),HN(v_{m},n))=0), and setting three parameters t=1t=1, ϵ=0\epsilon=0, and α=1\alpha=1 (as required by the structural-attack-resistance-only instance of the k​tkt-safe anonymization problem). This reduction transformation takes polynomial time. We can verify that the anonymized graph G′G^{\prime} is a kk-automorphism network with the minimal anonymization cost C​o​s​t​(G,G′)Cost(G,G^{\prime}), if and only if G′G^{\prime} is a produced k​tkt-safe graph with the minimal anonymization cost to the structural-attack-resistance-only instance of the k​tkt-safe anonymization problem. Thus, the structural-attack-resistance-only instance of the k​tkt-safe anonymization problem is NP-hard, and in turn the k​tkt-safety anonymization problem is also NP-hard.   \square\square

A-B Proof of Lemma V.1

Proof: Let g​e​d​(H​N​(vi,n),H​N​(vp,n))=d​i​s​t1ged(HN(v_{i},n),HN(v_{p},n))=dist_{1} and g​e​d​(H​N​(vm,n)CLOSE,ged(HN(v_{m},n), OPENH​N​(vp,n))HN(v_{p},n)) =d​i​s​t2=dist_{2}, based on triangle inequality, we have |d​i​s​t1−d​i​s​t2|≤g​e​d​(H​N​(vi,n),H​N​(vm,n))|dist_{1}-dist_{2}|\leq ged(HN(v_{i},n),HN(v_{m},n)). From the lemma assumption, |d​i​s​t1−d​i​s​t2|>ϵ|dist_{1}-dist_{2}|>\epsilon holds. By using the inequality transition, we can deduce that g​e​d​(H​N​(vi,n),H​N​(vm,n))>ϵged(HN(v_{i},n),HN(v_{m},n))>\epsilon, which violates the candidate set requirement (i.e., g​e​d​(H​N​(vi,n),H​N​(vm,n))ged(HN(v_{i},n),HN(v_{m},n)) ≤ϵ\leq\epsilon). Thus, vertex vmv_{m} cannot be in the candidate set vi.C​Sv_{i}.CS.   \square\square

A-C Attack Resistance Discussions on the Anonymized Graph via Algorithm 1

Attack Resistance Discussions on the Anonymized Graph via Algorithm 1. Note that, the anonymized k​tkt-safe graph via Algorithm 1 can resist from existing attacker models such as minimality attack [29]. Given a graph GG and its external knowledge defined in Definition 2, the anonymized k​tkt-safe graph G′G^{{}^{\prime}} of GG via Algorithm 1 will not suffer from the minimality attack, i.e., an attacker cannot locate any node and identify its sensitive attribute values with probabilities larger than 1/k1/k and α\alpha (as defined in Definition 4), respectively. The reasons for this are as follows. First, the one-to-one mapping of nodes between G′G^{{}^{\prime}} and GG does not hold here, which is the basis of minimality attack. This is because, instead of generalizing attribute values, we produce G′G^{{}^{\prime}} by inserting into GG duplicate/fake attributed nodes. Moreover, when releasing the resulting anonymized graph G′G^{\prime}, we will not release statistics of graph edit operators, such as the number of the inserted nodes/edges/attributes. As a result, the attacker cannot identify whether a node in k​tkt-safe graph G′G^{{}^{\prime}} is real or fake, and cannot uniquely identify any target vertex in G′G^{\prime} and its sensitive attribute values with high confidences.

A-D Graph Partitioning

Given a graph GG, the maximum size, γ\gamma, of subgraphs, and the number, ss, of partitions, Algorithm 5 produces a set, 𝒢\mathcal{G}, of partitioned subgraphs. Specifically, we will first check whether or not the number, |V⁡(G)||V(G)|, of vertices in a graph GG is larger than the maximum size γ\gamma. If |V⁡(G)|≤γ|V(G)|\leq\gamma holds for the original graph GG, we do not need to partition GG. If |V⁡(g)|≤γ|V(g)|\leq\gamma holds for a subgraph gg, we do not need to further partition gg. Since our anonymization process involves nn-hop neighbors of each vertex in GG, we will thus expand subgraph GG by including those vertices that are within nn hops away from border vertices in GG, and add the resulting expanded graph of GG to 𝒢\mathcal{G} (lines 2-6). When |V⁡(G)|>γ|V(G)|>\gamma holds, we partition graph GG based on the size and divide GG into ss subgraphs gig_{i} (1≤i≤s1\leq i\leq s) with similar sizes (i.e., |V⁡(gi)||V(g_{i})|), and partition each subgraph gig_{i} by recursively invoking function p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n​_​g​r​a​p​h​(⋅)partition\_graph(\cdot) (lines 7-10). Finally, we return the final partitioning set 𝒢\mathcal{G} (line 11).

A-E Discussions on Parameters γ\gamma and ss

Discussions on Parameters γ\gamma and ss. Parameters γ\gamma and ss are mainly used for the trade-off between the anonymization cost and efficiency. Intuitively, for larger γ\gamma (e.g., close to or even greater than |V⁡(G)||V(G)|) and/or smaller ss (e.g., close to 2), the partitioned subgraphs gi⊆Gg_{i}\subseteq G contain more vertices and each vertex in gig_{i} has more candidates (line 6 in Algorithm 1), which leads to lower anonymization cost and higher time cost to evaluate. On the other hand, with smaller γ\gamma (e.g., ≤\leq 1,000) and/or larger ss (e.g., ≥\geq 10), we need less time but higher anonymization cost to anonymize GG, since each vertex in gig_{i} has fewer candidates.

Moreover, the setup of γ\gamma and ss may also affect the usability of the anonymized graph. Given larger γ\gamma and/or smaller ss, the anonymized graph will have better usability, since there are fewer partitioned subgraphs with lower anonymization cost. Instead, smaller γ\gamma and/or larger ss will lead to worse usability of the anonymized graph. Therefore, for small graphs with fewer vertices, we can use larger γ\gamma (e.g., close to or even greater than |V⁡(G)||V(G)|) and/or smaller ss (e.g., close to 2) for a better utility with lower anonymization cost; for large graphs with unbearable anonymization time cost, we can use smaller γ\gamma (e.g., ≤\leq 1,000) and/or larger ss (e.g., ≥\geq 10) for a better efficiency.

A-F Candidate Set Detection

As illustrated in Algorithm 6, for each vertex vm∈V⁡(G)v_{m}\in V(G), we will first check whether or not vmv_{m} has the same quasi-identifier with viv_{i}, and the graph structure of the nn-hop neighbors, H​N​(vm,n)HN(v_{m},n), similar to that of viv_{i} (lines 3-4). If the answer is yes, we will add vmv_{m} to vi.C​Sv_{i}.CS as a potential candidate vertex in the protection set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS (line 5). Finally, we return the candidate set vi.C​Sv_{i}.CS (line 6).

A-G Discussions on Parameters kk, tt, ϵ\epsilon and α\alpha

Discussions on Parameters kk, tt, ϵ\epsilon and α\alpha. These 4 parameters are mainly related to the trade-off between privacy and usability of the anonymized graph. Specifically, in order to achieve a stronger privacy protection, we can set kk to a large value (e.g., ≥10\geq 10) and the other three to smaller values (e.g., close to 0), which in return may lead to worse usability. This is because, under this parameter setting, for each k​tkt-safe vertex viv_{i} in the anonymized graph, it requires that 1) its protection set vi.P​Sv_{i}.PS contains more vertices vi′v_{i}^{{}^{\prime}} (restricted by kk); 2) the value distributions between H​N​(vi,n)HN(v_{i},n) and HN(vi′,n)HN(v_{i}^{{}^{\prime}},n) on non-sensitive attributes are similar for each vi′∈vi.PSv_{i}^{{}^{\prime}}\in v_{i}.PS (restricted by tt); 3) the graph edit distance between H​N​(vi,n)HN(v_{i},n) and HN(vi′,n)HN(v_{i}^{{}^{\prime}},n) is small for each vi′∈vi.PSv_{i}^{{}^{\prime}}\in v_{i}.PS (restricted by ϵ\epsilon); and 4) a small fraction of vertices vi′∈vi.PSv_{i}^{{}^{\prime}}\in v_{i}.PS have sensitive values (restricted by α\alpha). As a result, we need to add more fake vertices and edges for a safer k​tkt-safe graph. The case of smaller kk and larger tt, ϵ\epsilon and α\alpha is opposite and omitted here.

A-H The Selection of a Pivot Set

The Selection of a Pivot Set. The basic idea of P​V​T​sPVTs selection is as follows. We sample a subgraph gsg_{s} from GG. Then, we select a pivot set P​V​T​sPVTs from GG that can prune a large number of vertices vm′∈gsv_{m}^{{}^{\prime}}\in g_{s} that cannot be the candidate of vi′.CSv_{i}^{{}^{\prime}}.CS for each vi′∈gsv_{i}^{{}^{\prime}}\in g_{s}. Finally, for each vertex viv_{i} in graph GG, we leverage the selected P​V​T​sPVTs to prune the vertex vm∈Gv_{m}\in G that are not in its candidate set vi.C​Sv_{i}.CS, which accelerate the execution of candidate set detection of Algorithm 6.

Specifically, given a graph GG, a sample graph size |V⁡(gs)||V(g_{s})|, an iteration threshold i​t​e​riter, and a pivot set size |P​V​T​s||PVTs|, Algorithm 7 illustrates the details of retrieving such a good pivot (vertex) set P​V​T​sPVTs. In particular, we have two variables, c​n​t.m​a​xcnt.max and c​n​t.n​o​wcnt.now, to record the maximum and current numbers of pruned vertices for different pivot sets in iterations, respectively, where vertices are pruned via Lemma V.1. Algorithm 7 first samples a subgraph gsg_{s} from GG (line 1). In the first iteration, we randomly select a pivot set P​V​T​sPVTs from GG and record the number of pruned vertices via Lemma V.1 (lines 6-11). In each of following iterations, we obtain a new pivot set p​v​t​spvts by randomly replacing an old pivot vp∈P​V​T​sv_{p}\in PVTs and recount the number of pruned vertices (lines 12-14). Finally, Algorithm 7 obtains and returns the pivot set which prunes the maximum number of vertices.
