Appendix B Description of Experimental Data Sets

Real data sets. We used six real-world graphs, C​o​r​aCora, D​B​L​PDBLP, E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions, F​a​c​e​b​o​o​kFacebook, W​i​k​i​p​e​d​i​aWikipedia, and A​r​x​i​vArxiv. C​o​r​aCora [27] contains 2,708 nodes (scientific publications from seven classes) and 5,278 edges (citations among these publications); D​B​L​PDBLP [37] is a co-author network from four research areas with 79,593 nodes (authors) and 201,334 edges (co-author relationships); E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions11 1 https://www.cse.msu.edu/~tangjili/datasetcode/truststudy.htm [26] contains 22,166 nodes (users) and 355,813 edges (trust relationships), crawled from viewer site Epinions in May, 2011; F​a​c​e​b​o​o​kFacebook22 2 http://snap.stanford.edu/data/ego-Facebook.html [17] contains 4,039 nodes (users addresses) and 88,234 edges (friendships), collected from survey participants; W​i​k​i​p​e​d​i​aWikipedia33 3 http://snap.stanford.edu/data/wiki-Vote.html [15] includes 7,115 nodes (users) and 103,689 edges (votes), from Wikipedia till January 2008; A​r​x​i​vArxiv44 4 https://snap.stanford.edu/data/ca-CondMat.html [16] has 23,133 nodes (authors) and 93,497 edges (co-authorships), collected from Condense Matter category in the period from January 1993 to April 2003. Note that, for all graphs, we treat them as undirected graphs.

For each publication (node) in C​o​r​aCora, we consider the number of unique vocabulary words it contains and the class it belongs to as its attributes. For each author (node) in D​B​L​PDBLP, we associate it with two attributes, prolific and research topics, where authors with ≥\geq 20, ≥10\geq 10 and <10<10 papers are labelled as highly prolific, prolific and low prolific, resp. For each user (node) in E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions, we randomly retrieve one rating item he/she gave, and set the attributes of this rating as the attributes of the node. The remaining three real data sets do not contain attribute values. Therefore, we fill the attribute values of vertices on F​a​c​e​b​o​o​kFacebook, W​i​k​i​p​e​d​i​aWikipedia, and A​r​x​i​vArxiv, with real values from Intel lab data55 5 http://db.csail.mit.edu/labdata/labdata.html, US & Canadian city weather data66 6 https://www.kaggle.com/selfishgene/historical-hourly-weather-data, and S&P 500 stock data77 7 https://www.kaggle.com/camnugent/sandp500, respectively. Specifically, I​n​t​e​lIntel contains 2.3 million data, collected from 54 sensors deployed in Intel Berkeley Research lab on Feb. 28-Apr. 5, 2014; W​e​a​t​h​e​rWeather contains 45.3​K45.3K historical weather (temperature) data for 30 US and Canadian Cities during 2012-2017; S​t​o​c​kStock has 619​K619K historical stock data for all companies found on the S&P 500 index till Feb. 2018. For each data set, we retrieved 4 attributes, where we consider 3 non-sensitive attributes and one sensitive attribute. Attribute values are normalized to integers from 0 to 5, which leads to at most 125 combinations of different quasi-identifiers.

Synthetic data sets. We produce 3 types of synthetic graph data containing 10,000 nodes, whose degree distributions follow uniform, Gaussian, or Zipf (a special case of heavy-tail) distribution, denoted as U​n​i​f​o​r​mUniform, G​a​u​s​s​i​a​nGaussian, and Z​i​p​fZipf, respectively, as shown in Table II. Specifically, U​n​i​f​o​r​mUniform holds nodes with degrees falling in [0,40][0,40], G​a​u​s​s​i​a​nGaussian generates nodes via a model taking 20 and 8 as mean and sigma, respectively, and Z​i​p​fZipf produces nodes with scale invariance 0.8. Moreover, for attributes, U​n​i​f​o​r​mUniform, G​a​u​s​s​i​a​nGaussian, and Z​i​p​fZipf data contain dd-dimensional (=4)(=4) attribute values, following uniform, Gaussian, and Zipf distributions, respectively, where each dimension takes 5 different values (0∼\sim5). Our codes for generating synthetic graphs are available at http://www.cs.kent.edu/~wren/kt-safety/.

Appendix C More Experimental Results

C-A Verification of the Cost Model and algorithms

Cost Model Verification for the Anonymization Cost Estimation via Eq. (3). We verify our cost model in Eq. (3) for estimating the cost of anonymizing a graph to be k​tkt-safe (Eq. (2) in Definition 6). Figure 8 illustrates the estimated anonymization cost of p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning on both real and synthetic data, where the retrieved sample graphs with 1,000 vertices and all parameters follow their default values in Table III. We also compare our estimated anonymization cost with the actual one (via p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning) on all data sets. From the figure, we can see that our proposed cost model can well estimate the anonymization cost of our proposed approach, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our cost model in Eq. (3).

Cost Evaluation of Selecting a Good Partitioning via Algorithm 4. Figure 9 shows the time cost of Algorithm 4 to select a good partitioning set of subgraphs on all tested data sets, where we vary the iteration number i​t​eite from 50 to 200. From the figure, as i​t​eite increases, the CPU time increases linearly. The partitioning strategy via Algorithm 4 is still efficient even when i​t​e=100ite=100 (e.g., <147.37<147.37 sec for D​B​L​PDBLP). Intuitively, more iterations will lead to a partitioning set with a low estimated anonymization cost. For all our experiments, we set i​t​eite to 50 by default, which can achieve a good partitioning set as evaluated in our cost model verification (Figure 8).

Cost Evaluation of Selecting a Good Pivot Set via Algorithm 7. Figure 10 reports the CPU time of selecting a set of 10 pivots on real/synthetic data via Algorithm 7, where we vary the iteration number from 100 to 400 and set the size of sample graphs to 1,000. From the figure, we can see that the time cost linearly increases as i​t​eite increases. When i​t​e=400ite=400, Algorithm 7 is still very efficient on all data sets (i.e., 2.882.88 sec ∼4.52\sim 4.52 sec). In this paper, we set i​t​eite to 100 by default. As shown in Figure 4(a), p​r​u​n​i​n​gpruning outperforms n​o​n​enone on all data sets, which demonstrates the effectiveness of the pivot set selection strategy via Algorithm 7.

Additional Cost Evaluation of the Generated k​tkt-Safe Graph. Table V demonstrates the anonymization and time costs of generating a k​tkt-safe graph on C​o​r​aCora via our p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning approach and that of producing a near optimal k​tkt-safe graph. Note that, there are |V⁡(G)|!|V(G)|! execution orders for producing a k​tkt-safe graph, which leads to an unbearable time cost to obtain the optimal anonymized graph. Instead, we randomly sample 3,000 (i.e., γ\gamma) different execution orders for producing a k​tkt-safe graph for C​o​r​aCora, and select the one with the lowest anonymization cost as the near optimal k​tkt-safe graph. From the table, we can see that the anonymized graph via our approach has a cost (i.e., 1031) similar to the near optimal one (i.e., 993). Moreover, our p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning approach needs less time cost than the one for generating the near optimal anonymized graph, where we estimate the near optimal time by summing up the total time of the 3,000 orders.

C-C More Efficiency Evaluation

A break-up cost analysis of p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning in Figure 4(a). Figure 15 illustrates the break-up cost of our p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning approach over C​o​r​aCora, D​B​L​PDBLP and E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions, which includes the partitioning cost (based on the cost model in Section V-A), candidate set generation cost (based on the pruning strategy in Section V-B and the k​tkt-tree in Section V-C), anonymization cost (based on Algorithm 2), and merging cost (based on Algorithm 3). From the figure, we can see that the partitioning part of p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning is the most time-consuming, since it needs to cluster vertices into different subgraphs. However, as shown in Figure 4(a), p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning outperforms p​r​u​n​i​n​gpruning and n​o​n​enone, in terms of the wall clock time, on large data sets, D​B​L​PDBLP and E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions, by 1-2 order of magnitude, which confirms the necessity of the partitioning for large graphs. On the other hand, it indicates that we may not need to apply the partitioning strategy for small graphs (e.g., C​o​r​aCora). Moreover, the anonymization part is the second most time-consuming, as it needs to anonymize each vertex to a k​tkt-safe one.

More Efficiency Evaluation vs. Wall Clock Time. Figure 16 illustrates the wall clock time of anonymizing the graph for F​a​c​e​b​o​o​kFacebook, W​i​k​i​p​e​d​i​aWikipedia, A​r​x​i​vArxiv, U​n​i​f​o​r​mUniform, G​a​u​s​s​i​a​nGaussian and Z​i​p​fZipf, where default values of parameters are used for synthetic data. From the figure, we can see that p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning needs the least wall clock time on all data sets, which confirms the efficiency of our graph anonymization approach. For the three variants of our methods, similar as Figure 4(a), p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​npartition has the smallest wall clock time on all data sets except F​a​c​e​b​o​o​kFacebook, followed by p​r​u​n​i​n​gpruning and n​o​n​enone, respectively. Specifically, p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​npartition is slower than p​r​u​n​i​n​gpruning on F​a​c​e​b​o​o​kFacebook, which indicates that we may not need to adopt the partitioning strategy on small graph with less vertices.

Efficiency vs. identity privacy threshold kk. Figure 17 illustrates the performance of our p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning method over both real and synthetic data sets, where k=5k=5, 1010, 1515 and 2020 and other parameters are set as their default values in Table III. From the figure, with larger kk, the wall clock time slightly increase over all data sets, since each node needs to find more similar candidates for a stronger privacy guarantee. Specifically, the p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning approach achieves the highest time cost on DBLP on all kk values, since DBLP has the largest number of vertices. Nevertheless, our p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning still needs low time cost (less than 163.78 s​e​csec even when k=20k=20).

Efficiency vs. sensitive privacy threshold α\alpha. From the figure, when α\alpha increases, the wall clock time slightly decreases, since there will be more tolerable sensitive attribute values in the protection set of each node (as defined in Definition 4). Nevertheless, D​B​L​PDBLP still has the highest time cost due to the large size of vertices.

Efficiency vs. graph edit distance threshold ϵ\epsilon. Figure 19 reports the performance of our p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning method, by varying ϵ\epsilon from 3 to 7, where other parameters are set to their defaults. From the result, when ϵ\epsilon increases, the wall clock time decreases. This is because, with larger ϵ\epsilon, there will be more initial detected candidates for each node (via Algorithm 6), which needs less time for obtaining the node’s protection sets.

Efficiency vs. distance threshold tt. Figure 20 demonstrates the effect of the distance threshold tt on our p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning method on real and synthetic data sets, where t=0.1t=0.1, 0.20.2, 0.30.3 and 0.40.4 and other parameters are set as their defaults. From the figure, when tt increases, the time cost decrease on all data sets. Intuitively, with larger tt, there will be more initial candidate nodes (obtained via Algorithm 6) satisfying the requirements of k​tkt-safety model, due to the requirement loosing of distribution similarity of n-hop neighbors between graph nodes.

Scalability Evaluation vs. Graph Size |V⁡(G)||V(G)|. Figure 21 tests the scalability of our approach, p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning, on synthetic graphs, where |V⁡(G)||V(G)| varies from 10​K10K to 100​K100K and other parameters are set to their default values. From figures, we can see that the wall clock time of p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning increases for larger |V⁡(G)||V(G)|. Even when |V⁡(G)|=100​K|V(G)|=100K, the time cost is still acceptable (i.e., 208.51 s​e​c∼sec\sim 260.17 s​e​csec). Furthermore, our p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning approach over U​n​i​f​o​r​mUniform data can achieve the lowest time cost. This is because, G​a​u​s​s​i​a​nGaussian has the largest average node degree, and Z​i​p​fZipf has more nodes with sensitive values (i.e., small attribute values), which require more time cost.

Efficiency vs. the maximum size, γ\gamma, of subgraphs. From the figure, when γ\gamma increases, the time cost increases. This is because, with larger γ\gamma, it needs to check more vertices for obtaining the protection set for each vertex in subgraphs. Nevertheless, the time cost of our p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning approach is still acceptable even when γ=2,000\gamma=2,000 (i.e., 172.86172.86 sec for D​B​L​PDBLP). Efficiency vs. the number, ss, of graph partitions. Figure 23 reports the wall clock time of our p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning approach, by varying ss from 22 to 66, where other parameters are set to their default values. From the figure, with larger ss, our approach achieves lower time cost. The reason for this is that, with larger ss, there will be more subgraphs with fewer nodes, each of which needs lower time to be anonymized.

C-D More Anonymization Cost Evaluation

More Anonymization Cost Evaluation. Figure 24 illustrates the anonymization cost of all the approaches on F​a​c​e​b​o​o​kFacebook, W​i​k​i​p​e​d​i​aWikipedia, A​r​x​i​vArxiv, U​n​i​f​o​r​mUniform, G​a​u​s​s​i​a​nGaussian and Z​i​p​fZipf. Similar as Figure 4(b), p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning and p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​npartition have slightly higher cost than p​r​u​n​i​n​gpruning and n​o​n​enone, since our approach needs to add more fake nodes on the partitioned subgraphs than that of the original single graph to make each vertex as k​tkt-safe.

The anonymization cost vs. identity privacy threshold kk. Figure 25 shows the effect of the privacy threshold kk on our p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning approach over real and synthetic data sets, where kk varies from 55 to 2020 and other parameters are set as their default (bold) values in Table III. From the figure, when kk increases, the anonymization cost increases. This is reasonable, since larger kk indicates stronger privacy power and larger size of protection set for each graph node. Specifically, the p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning approach achieves the highest anonymization cost on E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions on all kk values. After we carefully examined E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions, we found that it has the largest size of quasi-identifiers, which leads to less candidates in protection set (Definition 3) for each vertex. As a result, our approach needs more anonymization cost to make each graph vertex as a k​tkt-safe one. Nevertheless, the anonymization cost of our p​a​r​t​i​t​i​o​n+p​r​u​n​i​n​gpartition+pruning method is still reasonable (less than 176,523 even when k=20k=20).

The anonymization cost vs. sensitive privacy threshold α\alpha. From the result, when α\alpha increases, the anonymization cost decreases, since larger α\alpha indicates more tolerance of sensitive values in protection set of graph nodes. Nevertheless, E​p​i​n​i​o​n​sEpinions still needs the highest anonymization cost due to the large size of quasi-identifiers.

The anonymization cost vs. graph edit distance threshold ϵ\epsilon. From the figure, when ϵ\epsilon increases, the anonymization cost smoothly decreases, since we can find more candidates for each node and need less graph operations.

The anonymization cost vs. distance threshold tt. The anonymization cost vs. size, |V⁡(G)||V(G)|, of graph GG.
